title: Knowing Where Well Enough to Grasp: An Error Budget From Base to Fingertip, the Chance a Grasp Works, and the Camera That Takes the Base Out of It

questions.question: How do independent errors combine?
options: They add: the worst case of each, summed
Only the largest matters, and the rest can be dropped
They average, since they are independent
In quadrature: the square root of the sum of squares
questions.explanation: For independent errors the variances add, so the standard deviations combine as the root of the sum of squares. The largest dominates but the others are still in it.

questions.question: The hand's sigma came to:
questions.explanation: 20 mm of position and 16 mm from a degree of heading at 0.9 m, in quadrature with the small terms, is 25.6 mm. The arm's 0.1 mm does not show.

questions.question: The chance of a good grasp with a tolerance of 10 mm was:
questions.explanation: A tolerance of 10 mm is about 0.4 of the hand's sigma of 25.6 mm. 20000 simulated grasps gave the same 0.30.

questions.question: With a camera on the hand the chance was:
questions.explanation: With the camera's 2 mm and the arm's 0.1 mm the sigma was 2.0 mm, a fifth of the tolerance, and the chance rounds to 1.000.

questions.question: Why does the camera help so much?
options: Its error is smaller than the arm's repeatability
It measures the part relative to the hand, so the base's errors are not in it
It lets the base stop more accurately
It averages many pictures of the part
questions.explanation: The camera sees the part from the hand. Where the base stopped and how it was turned no longer enter the measurement.

questions.question: How many sigmas make 99 percent?
questions.explanation: 1.96 sigmas give 95 percent and 2.58 give 99. For 99 percent of grasps within 10 mm the sigma has to be 3.9 mm.
